items.title: The science-to-practice gap in allergology: a critical appraisal of determinants and knowledge-translation strategies across health systems.
items.abstract: Evidence-based medicine assumes that high-quality research, once produced, will reach the bedside. In allergology this assumption is repeatedly violated. Solid evidence accumulates while its uptake in daily practice remains incomplete and variable across health systems. This critical appraisal characterizes the science-to-practice gap in allergology using current data, drawn from a search of PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library covering January 2015 to March 2026. It examines the gap's determinants across institutional and economic contexts and evaluates knowledge-translation (KT) strategies with the strongest evidence base. ARIA, GINA, and EAACI adherence is quantified for allergic rhinitis, asthma, and AIT, with AIT uptake estimates treated as setting-specific rather than universal. Four determinant domains, education, conflicts of interest, reimbursement, and local adaptation, are compared across high-income EU countries, the UK, and low- and middle-income countries, and five KT strategies are appraised. The gap is measurable, clinically consequential, and modifiable. Its persistence reflects structural and policy factors more than clinician knowledge. Combinations of audit-and-feedback and academic detailing, tailored to local environments and supported by clinical decision tools, offer the most durable improvement documented to date. Allergological societies should integrate implementation science and independent conflict-of-interest management into their strategic priorities. The science-to-practice gap in allergology is a structural, measurable deficit, not an occasional lapse, and it is best understood as an implementation problem rather than a knowledge problem.Only about 15% of patients with allergic rhinitis are treated in full accordance with ARIA recommendations. Adherence is higher among ENT specialists than general practitioners, locating much of the gap at the primary-care and specialist interface.Allergen immunotherapy, the only disease-modifying treatment for IgE-mediated respiratory allergic disease, is used by only a minority of patients in the available real-world evidence. Several primary-care settings report uptake below 10%, measured against setting-specific rather than uniformly defined eligibility criteria, and reimbursement structure is descriptively associated with prescribing.Four modifiable determinants are associated with the gap, namely industry-weighted continuing education, financial conflicts of interest in guideline panels, reimbursement design, and the absence of locally adapted clinical pathways.Audit-and-feedback combined with academic detailing produces the largest and most durable gains documented in the reviewed literature. Clinical decision support and local adaptation workshops add value when integrated into workflow and local context. - Priorities for the field include a validated cross-system adherence measure, independent conflict-of-interest management comparable to cardiology, and a shift from guideline translation to context mapping in low-resource settings.

items.title: Reply - Letter to the editor: Interpreting the effects of protocolized nutrition in critically ill adults.
Lipoprotein(a) management simplified: The National Lipid Association lipid simplified series.
items.abstract: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a unique apolipoprotein B-containing lipoprotein, similar to low-density lipoproteins. Plasma concentrations of Lp(a) are largely genetically determined. High Lp(a) levels are recognized as a causal and independent risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and are an important contributor to residual ASCVD risk. International guidelines reflect the importance of measuring Lp(a) at least once in all adults as an important component of ASCVD risk assessment and management. This document aims to summarize the guidelines recommending universal measurement of Lp(a), including the associated risk thresholds that can be used to identify individuals with higher ASCVD risk based on their plasma Lp(a) concentrations. Additionally, direction on managing patients with high Lp(a) is provided, as well as information on therapies in development to lower Lp(a). The most recent statements and updates from international societies were reviewed for guidance on Lp(a) measurement and management, with particular attention to the 2026 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association multisociety guideline on the management of dyslipidemia. Information on pharmaceutical agents that are in late stages of development for targeted lowering of Lp(a) is also summarized. The synthesis of existing information on how to manage patients with elevated Lp(a) reinforces the importance of measurement of Lp(a) in all adults at least once in their lifetime and provides direction on when repeated measurement may be warranted. In the absence of available drugs to specifically and effectively lower Lp(a), management of modifiable risk factors is encouraged. Furthermore, the large contribution of genetics to the determination of Lp(a) levels underscores the importance of cascade screening of family members to identify at-risk individuals. There is broad recognition of the importance of measuring Lp(a) at least once in all adults, owing to the recognized role of elevated Lp(a) as an important ASCVD risk enhancer. At present, this information is useful in risk stratification and can guide optimal management of ASCVD risk in patients. However, the potential for new Lp(a) lowering therapies to specifically and substantially reduce Lp(a) levels underscores the importance of Lp(a) measurement in all adults.

items.title: Need for population-specific lipid guidelines for South Asians: Focus on the Indian population and its distinct cardiometabolic risk profile.
items.abstract: South Asian individuals bear a disproportionately high burden of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), characterized by earlier onset, greater severity, and higher mortality compared with Western populations. This is despite lower average low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels and is driven by a distinctive cardiometabolic phenotype, including adverse lifestyle factors, high prevalence of insulin resistance and diabetes, hypertriglyceridemia, increased small dense LDL particles, elevated lipoprotein(a), and low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) levels. To review the cardiometabolic risk profile of South Asians and the rationale for population-specific lipid management strategies, with a focus on contemporary evidence and recommendations from the Lipid Association of India (LAI). The relevant evidence was identified from published prospective cohort studies, randomized controlled trials, meta-analyses, and international and Indian guidelines with emphasis on studies evaluating South Asian/ Indian populations. The literature was evaluated with specific attention to differences in ASCVD burden, age at disease onset, cardiometabolic risk factors, lipid and lipoprotein profiles, and treatment responses between South Asian/Indian and Western populations. Evidence supporting intensive LDL-C lowering and combination lipid-lowering therapy was reviewed. South Asians demonstrate a high prevalence of atherogenic dyslipidemia characterized by hypertriglyceridemia, low HDL-C, elevated non-HDL-C, and increased apolipoprotein B (apo B) containing particles, often with relatively modest LDL-C levels. Western risk prediction models and lipid thresholds may therefore underestimate ASCVD risk in this population. LAI guidelines recommend lower LDL-C targets than Western counterparts, refined ASCVD risk stratification including extreme-risk group categories, and the use of non-HDL-C and apo B as complementary therapeutic targets. Combination lipid-lowering therapy with statins, ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, and proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitors is often required to achieve recommended goals and address residual lipid-related risk. Given the distinctive cardiometabolic profile and high ASCVD burden, population-specific lipid guidelines are essential. Intensive LDL-C and non-HDL-C lowering, comprehensive risk stratification, and early combination therapy, alongside sustained lifestyle modification and optimal management of comorbidities, are key strategies to mitigate the growing epidemic of ASCVD in South Asian populations.

items.title: Integrated Single-Cell and Spatial Multi-Omics Reveal S100A12 + Neutrophil Reprogramming Across Oral Inflammatory States and Immunotherapy-Associated Perturbation.
items.abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) develops through a continuum of tissue states from chronic inflammation and potentially malignant lesions to invasive cancer, yet the dynamic remodeling of the oral immune microenvironment and its relevance to immunotherapy-associated inflammation remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, murine immunotherapy datasets, and experimental validation to characterize immune and stromal alterations across healthy mucosa, periodontitis, leukoplakia, and OSCC. This integrated analysis revealed distinct oral immune microenvironment states and identified condition-associated neutrophil programs, including an S100A12-enriched inflammatory state, an S100A14-associated metabolic state in leukoplakia, and tumor-associated neutrophil states in OSCC. Spatial analyses and cell-cell communication modeling further nominated immune-stromal interaction networks involving S100A12 + neutrophils and fibroblast-associated inflammatory signaling. A machine-learning framework identified a nine-gene Neu_S100A12-associated signature that discriminated periodontitis-associated inflammatory states across two retrospective cohorts, with seven concordantly upregulated genes prioritized for biological validation. Multiplex immunofluorescence and an IFN-γ-primed OSCC inflammatory model provided experimental support for a TNF-associated inflammatory phenotype linked to the S100A12 program. Together, these findings establish a cross-sectional multi-omics framework for defining oral immune states and identify S100A12-associated neutrophil programs as candidate mediators of oral inflammation and immunotherapy-related immune perturbation, providing a foundation for future prospective and mechanistic studies.

items.title: Relapse After Dupilumab Discontinuation in Pediatric Moderate-to-Severe Atopic Dermatitis: A Single-Center Retrospective Study From China.
items.abstract: Dupilumab has been demonstrated to be an effective and safe treatment for atopic dermatitis (AD) in pediatric patients in clinical trials. However, data on postdiscontinuation relapse are scarce. This study aimed to describe relapse patterns and explore factors associated with relapse after dupilumab discontinuation in pediatric patients with moderate-to-severe AD. This retrospective study included 37 children treated with dupilumab for at least 16 weeks. Of these, 35 discontinued dupilumab and entered postdiscontinuation follow-up through May 2025. Relapse-free survival was evaluated using the Kaplan-Meier method. A prespecified exploratory Cox model including age at AD onset and baseline absolute eosinophil count was fitted using complete cases. An exploratory logistic regression analysis was reported separately as a supplementary analysis. Among the 35 patients who entered postdiscontinuation follow-up, 27 (77.1%) experienced relapse. The overall median relapse-free survival time was 150 days (95% CI, 120-240 days). No statistically significant difference was observed between dupilumab monotherapy and dupilumab plus subcutaneous immunotherapy (log-rank P = 0.709). In the prespecified two-variable Cox model, the estimated relapse hazards were lower with later age at AD onset (HR = 0.76; 95% CI, 0.54-1.07; P = 0.115) and higher baseline eosinophil count (HR = 0.39; 95% CI, 0.13-1.18; P = 0.094), but neither association reached statistical significance. Relapse was common after dupilumab discontinuation in this small retrospective cohort. The directions of the Cox estimates suggest that age at AD onset and baseline eosinophil count may warrant further investigation, but the current data do not establish either variable as a predictor of relapse. Larger prospective studies are required.

items.title: Emerging landscape of antibody-drug conjugates in lung cancer: a clinical review.
items.abstract: Lung cancer is a heterogeneous disease, and while targeted therapies and immunotherapies have improved patient outcomes, 5-year overall survival remains poor at approximately 20%. Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) target tumors using a targeted antibody that delivers a cytotoxic payload with clinically proven antitumor activity, and over a dozen ADCs are under consideration for solid tumors. Recent clinical trial data in metastatic non-small cell lung cancer have led to FDA approval of three ADCs: trastuzumab deruxtecan for patients with human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-mutated disease, telisotuzumab vedotin for MET-overexpressing tumors, and datopotamab deruxtecan for patients with epidermal growth factor receptor-mutated disease. In this article, we review the trajectory of individual ADC targets in lung cancer, describe the latest clinical trial results, and discuss future innovations in ADC therapies and potential mechanisms of resistance.

[Effects of gambogic acid on liver function in rats with chronic hepatitis B by adjusting Sirt1/FoxO1 pathway].
items.abstract: This study investigated the effects of gambogic acid(GA) on liver function in rats with chronic hepatitis B(CHB) via the silent information regulator 2 homolog 1(Sirt1)/forkhead box transcription factor O1(FoxO1) signaling pathway. A CHB rat model was established using hepatitis B virus(HBV) antigen. Another 10 healthy rats injected with an equal volume of physiological saline served as the control group. After successful modeling, rats were divided into a CHB group, low-dose GA(L-GA, 50 mg·kg~(-1) GA by gavage) group, high-dose GA(H-GA, 100 mg·kg~(-1) GA by gavage) group, and GA+EX527(100 mg·kg~(-1) GA by gavage combined with intraperitoneal injection of 5 mg·kg~(-1) EX527, a Sirt1 inhibitor) group. Rats in the control and CHB groups received equal volumes of physiological saline by gavage and intraperitoneal injection. Each group consisted of 10 rats, and treatment was administered once daily for 4 consecutive weeks. Serum levels of aspartate aminotransferase(AST), alanine aminotransferase(ALT), and total bilirubin(TBIL) were measured using an automated biochemical analyzer. ELISA was performed to determine the serum levels of interleukin-1β(IL-1β) and tumor necrosis factor-α(TNF-α). RT-qPCR was used to detect viral expression in liver tissue. HE staining was performed to observe pathological changes in liver tissue, and Masson staining was used to evaluate hepatic fibrosis. Western blot was used to detect the protein expression of Sirt1 and acetylated(Ac)-FoxO1/Fox O1 in liver tissue. The results showed that liver tissue in the CHB group exhibited marked swelling, disordered cellular arrangement, extensive inflammatory cell infiltration, and collagen deposition. Treatment with L-GA and H-GA progressively alleviated pathological injury and collagen deposition in liver tissue, whereas pathological injury and collagen deposition were further aggravated in the GA+EX527 group. Compared with the control group, the CHB group showed significantly increased levels of ALT, AST, TBIL, IL-1β, TNF-α, and HBV DNA, and significantly decreased expression of Sirt1 and Ac-FoxO1/Fox O1(P<0. 05). Compared with the CHB group, the L-GA and H-GA groups showed significantly decreased levels of ALT, AST, TBIL, IL-1β, TNF-α, and HBV DNA, and significantly increased expression of Sirt1 and Ac-FoxO1/Fox O1(P<0. 05), with more pronounced changes observed in the H-GA group(P<0. 05). Treatment with GA+EX527 significantly reversed the changes in the above indicators observed in the H-GA group(P<0. 05). In conclusion, GA may improve liver function in CHB rats by activating the Sirt1/Fox O1 signaling pathway, thereby inhibiting inflammatory responses and hepatic fibrosis and reducing viral expression in liver tissue.

items.title: Effectiveness and safety of three years of bulevirtide monotherapy in patients with HDV-related compensated cirrhosis: the Italian compassionate use program.
items.abstract: Bulevirtide (BLV) monotherapy for up to 144 weeks was safe and effective in patients with chronic hepatitis D (CHD) in a phase III trial, but long-term real-world data are limited. We evaluated its effectiveness and safety in patients with HDV-related cirrhosis in clinical practice. Consecutive patients with HDV-related cirrhosis treated with BLV 2 mg/day monotherapy through the Italian compassionate use program were included. Virological (VR), biochemical (BR), and combined responses (CR), undetectable HDV RNA, virological and biochemical breakthroughs (VBK and BBK), non-invasive tests (NITs), safety, and liver-related events were assessed. Ninety-seven patients were enrolled: median age, 52 years (interquartile range, 40-61); 53% were male; 96% were European; and 92% had Child-Pugh class A cirrhosis. VR, BR, CR, and HDV RNA target-not-detected/below-the-limit-of-detection rates increased over time, with 144-week cumulative incidences of 77%, 84%, 64%, and 53%, respectively. Overall, 11% and 5% of patients experienced a VBK and BBK, respectively. LSM, APRI, FIB-4, and LSPS, but not SSM, declined significantly during therapy. The 3-year cumulative probabilities of decompensation and HCC were 1.3% (95% CI, 1-3%) and 10% (95% CI, 4-19%), respectively. Treatment was well tolerated. Long-term BLV 2 mg/day monotherapy was safe and effective in patients with cirrhosis. Response rates increased over time, while decompensating events remained uncommon.

items.title: Empowerment in advanced liver disease: UK experiences of care from the perspectives of people with lived experience, carers and healthcare professionals.
items.abstract: ObjectivesLiver disease is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality, with alcohol-related liver disease, metabolic-associated steatotic liver disease, and viral hepatitis comprising most cases in the UK. Advanced liver disease presents challenges due to unpredictable disease trajectories, high symptom burden, psychosocial impacts, and stigma. This study aimed to develop an explanatory theory of care experiences in decompensated advanced liver disease from the perspectives of individuals living with the condition, carers, and healthcare professionals, with public involvement embedded throughout.MethodsUsing Charmaz's Constructivist Grounded Theory methodology, semi-structured interviews were conducted across the UK with individuals with advanced liver disease, carers, and healthcare professionals. Data collection and analysis occurred concurrently using constant comparison, focused coding, memoing, and theoretical sampling.ResultsTwenty-four people participated in interviews. Analysis generated the Empowerment Continuum, an explanatory theory conceptualising empowerment as a dynamic, relational process shaped by personal, relational, and systemic factors. Five conceptual categories informed the theory: self-care, navigating healthcare services, healthcare professionals' contributions, carers' involvement and support, and information and communication.DiscussionThe Empowerment Continuum provides a framework for understanding care experiences in advanced liver disease. Supporting empowerment requires collaborative, accessible, and person-centred approaches involving people with liver disease, carers, and healthcare professionals.

items.title: Dietary safflower seed oil supplementation modulates antiviral immunity in specific-pathogen-free chickens infected with fowl adenovirus serotype 8a.
items.abstract: Fowl adenovirus serotype 8a (FAdV-8a) is an important cause of inclusion body hepatitis in chickens, but nutritional strategies for enhancing host resistance remain poorly characterized. This study evaluated whether dietary supplementation with safflower seed oil affected growth performance, viral burden, and immune responses in specific-pathogen-free chickens infected with FAdV-8a. Chickens received a basal diet containing 1% corn oil or the same diet containing 1% safflower seed oil and were inoculated oculonasally with 10⁶ TCID₅₀ of the low-virulence FAdV-8a strain JL/170408 at 21 d of age. Safflower seed oil increased average daily gain during days 1-21 and average daily feed intake during days 1-21 and 21-45, without affecting feed conversion ratio. The safflower seed oil group developed an earlier antibody peak (12 vs. 16 dpi) and generally higher antibody levels. Hepatic viral DNA loads were lower in safflower seed oil-fed birds at 3 and 7 dpi, whereas differences in viral DNA loads in other tissues were limited. Safflower seed oil also produced tissue- and time-dependent changes in avian β-defensins, Toll-like receptors, cytokines, antioxidant-related genes, NF-κB signaling molecules, PPAR-γ, CD4, and CD8. Overall, safflower seed oil supplementation was associated with improved early growth, enhanced FAdV-specific antibody responses, lower hepatic viral DNA loads, and broad transcriptional changes in immune- and antioxidant-related pathways. These findings support a modulatory effect of safflower seed oil on antiviral immune responses, while the underlying mechanisms require direct functional validation.

items.title: IHPBA 2026 global guideline for the management of hepatocellular carcinoma in resource-constrained healthcare settings.
items.abstract: Current guidelines for the management of patients with HCC are predominantly focused on well-resourced healthcare systems. In 2024, the IHPBA Legacy committee initiated a process to develop global resource-sensitive guidelines for the management of HCC. An IHPBA global guideline group produced and circulated statements on the management of HCC from diagnosis to treatment, discussed these in online webinars and generated guidelines. This document focuses on the diagnosis and management of patients with HCC in resource-constrained healthcare settings. Initial diagnosis by ultrasound is supported by cross-sectional imaging. Alfa-feto protein and assessment of liver synthetic function are recommended at diagnosis. Lesion biopsy is not mandated. Liver resection is the recommended treatment of choice for single HCC in patients with preserved liver function and up to 3 lesions ≤3 cm. Radiofrequency and microwave are regarded as equivalent and can be used if resection is not available. Ethanol injection can be used if thermal ablation is not available but should be restricted to small lesions. TACE and TAE can be used for intermediate stage disease. Atezolizumab/bevacizumab combination is recommended as first line systemic therapy with sorafenib and Lenvatinib being recommended if first line is not an option. Advice for the care of the patient with advanced or terminal disease is provided. This document provides resource-sensitive HCC guidelines that prioritise feasibility, maximise benefit, and reduce default reliance on best supportive care alone and are produced for the IHPBA by discussion with the global community of IHPBA.

Cinnamic Acid Attenuates Ethanol-Exacerbated Hepatocyte Pyroptosis in Type 2 Diabetes via AMPK-Mediated NLRP3/GSDMD Inhibition.
items.abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is frequently accompanied by chronic ethanol (ET) consumption, which worsens metabolic dysregulation and organ damage. Cinnamic acid (CA), a natural compound with anti-diabetic and hepatoprotective effects, shows therapeutic potential, but its role in mitigating ET-exacerbated hepatocyte injury in diabetes remains unclear. This study thus investigated whether CA protects against ET-induced hepatocyte pyroptosis under diabetic conditions and explored the underlying mechanisms. In vitro, HepG2 cells cultured under high-glucose (HG) conditions were exposed to ET to simulate a diabetic state with concomitant alcohol intake. Pyroptosis was evaluated by morphological examination and annexin V/PI staining. The involvement of the NACHT, LRR and PYD domains-containing protein 3 (NLRP3)/gasdermin D (GSDMD) pathway and AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) activation was assessed via immunoblotting, reactive oxygen species (ROS) detection, and molecular docking. In vivo, a T2DM mouse model was established using a high-fat diet combined with streptozotocin injection, followed by ET exposure and CA treatment. Metabolic parameters, histopathological changes, and hepatic signaling pathways were analyzed. Our results showed that ET exposure significantly increased pyroptotic body formation, ROS production, and NLRP3/GSDMD pathway activation in HG-treated HepG2 cells-all of which were reversed by CA in a concentration-dependent manner. Mechanistically, CA directly bound to and activated AMPK, and the protective effects were abolished by the AMPK inhibitor Compound C. In T2DM mice, ET exposure aggravated insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, hepatic steatosis, and histopathological abnormalities, whereas CA intervention ameliorated these adverse effects and modulated the AMPK-NLRP3/GSDMD signaling axis in liver tissue. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that CA alleviates ET-exacerbated hepatocyte pyroptosis under diabetic conditions by activating AMPK and subsequently inhibiting the NLRP3/GSDMD signaling cascade. This study provides novel insights into the therapeutic potential of CA in T2DM complicated by alcoholic hepatocellular injury.

items.title: Regulatory B Cells: Beyond Antibody Production in Immunity and Cancer.
items.abstract: B lymphocytes, which originally develop in the bone marrow, are key components of humoral immunity and are responsible for antibody production. B lymphocytes arise from progenitor B cells (pro-B cells), which are located in the fetal liver during early development and are generated predominantly in the bone marrow before birth. Based on their stage of maturation and function, B cells are divided into many subsets. B cells play a critical role in the humoral immune response through antibody secretion; however, accumulating evidence indicates that B cells also have more diverse functions in the immune system. Different B cell subsets can modulate effector T-cell responses through antigen presentation, costimulation, and cytokine production. A distinct subpopulation of B cells, termed regulatory B cells (Bregs), negatively regulates cellular immune responses and contributes to the control of inflammation, infectious diseases, autoimmunity, and cancer. These cells may represent viable targets for therapeutic manipulation or immunomodulation independent of antibody production. In this review, we discuss the various B cell subsets and describe non-humoral functions of B cells, with particular emphasis on regulatory B cells and their roles in immunological diseases and cancer.

items.title: CD58: A Promising Diagnostic and Prognostic Biomarker for Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
items.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a global health challenge due to the lack of reliable early diagnostic markers and therapeutic targets. While CD58 is implicated in immune modulation and cancer progression, its role in HCC has not been fully explored. Bioinformatics analysis was performed to assess CD58 expression and its clinical significance. Immunohistochemistry was conducted on tissue microarrays to validate CD58 expression, while enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay was used to measure soluble CD58 levels in HCC serum. A nomogram was constructed to predict overall survival, and decision curve analysis along with area under the ROC curve were applied to evaluate its diagnostic value. Additionally, serum trace elemental levels were analyzed using inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy to explore their relationship with sCD58. CD58 was overexpressed in human HCC tissues and its expression was associated with age and hepatitis status. For HCC patients, CD58 was identified as an independent prognostic factor. Furthermore, CD58 was positively correlated with T cell infiltration in HCC tissues. The levels of sCD58 were elevated in HCC serum and showed significant diagnostic potential. Notably, sCD58 correlated with copper levels, providing new insights into its role in HCC progression. CD58 is a promising diagnostic and prognostic biomarker for HCC, and targeting CD58 may offer novel therapeutic strategies. The correlation between sCD58 and copper levels suggests that copper could play a key role in HCC pathogenesis.
